claims.text: Percolating chemical short-range-order clusters in single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloys cause a nonlinear reduction in thermal conductivity.
The conductivity reduction exceeds predictions from standard scattering models.
The proposed reduction is driven by a topological transition in phonon mean free path rather than simple point-defect scattering.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr-type alloy is a single-phase bcc random solid solution.
Thermal annealing or rapid quenching can induce nucleation and growth of SRO clusters until they form a connected network.
The alloy remains single-phase bcc in the proposed high-temperature operating regime.
A percolating SRO network acts as a topological barrier to phonon propagation.
SRO-network percolation alters effective-medium behavior beyond simple volume averaging.
Percolating SRO clusters create either a continuous path of high scattering potential or a phononic-bandgap-like effect.
The proposed continuous scattering path or bandgap-like effect causes a sharp decrease in thermal conductivity.
Standard serial/parallel mixing models assume isolated scatterers and therefore cannot capture the proposed percolation-driven conductivity drop.
Thermal conductivity will decrease abruptly at a specific SRO volume fraction corresponding to the percolation threshold.
The conductivity-versus-SRO trend will deviate significantly from the linear or quadratic trends predicted by standard scattering models.
Standard potential functions represent the baseline as a random solid solution or as isolated SRO clusters modeled through Matthiessen's rule or effective-medium approximations.
The proposed effect applies only when SRO clusters physically percolate in a single-phase bcc system and does not apply after phase separation or below the percolation threshold.
The potential-energy surface must capture SRO evolution accurately to predict the onset of percolation.
Machine-learning potentials can be used to track the percolation threshold of SRO clusters explicitly.
A conductivity curve that follows a standard effective-medium trend without an inflection at SRO percolation would falsify the proposed percolative mechanism.
